data.name: Damn virgins
data.detailed_description:
Seven virgins will be sacrified unless you help them!

Just to clarify, your help is only needed to avoid the sacrifice, solving their virginity problem is a bit more complicated as you will discover.

FMV adventure inspired in classic adventure games. Solving puzzles usually unlocks a videoclip that reveals the plot.

Synopsis: On the 21st of December, 2012, just as the Mayans predicted, the world ended nothing happened. Alex, the dean of a small university believes otherwise and concocts an evil plan.

Plot


The Mayans told that life is governed in cycles of 5200 years. When each cycle ends, the seven gods who created mankind allow the cycle to repeat in return for an offering.

Seven virgins must be sacrificed, one for each god.



Approximately 5200 years ago, the offering was demanded by the gods. But during the sacrifice, something went wrong. Enraged, the gods punished the Mayan people, who then disappeared. This disappearance wasn't immediate, though. Earthquakes, droughts, and volcanic eruptions came one after the other, ultimately leading to the fall of the empire.



In the present day, the gods returned to claim what was theirs, but the Mayans are no longer around to perform the sacrifices. Alex, the dean of a small university, lives in distress over this, and when the appointed date, December 21, 2012, arrives, he starts to lose his mind. In the following months, he starts collecting news about natural disasters: eruptions, earthquakes, hurricanes. Things that were always there, but his sick mind connects them with the wrath of the gods over not receiving their gift. Alex therefore decides to do the sacrifices himself.

The problem is that today, virgins are really hard to find.



Using his position, he founds a fraternity in his university and tricks the dumbest virgin boys that he finds into joining. Alex promises them that if they finish their studies, he'll take them to Riviera Maya as an end-of-term trip. Using an outing as a ruse, he plans to sacrifice them at the top of Chichen Itza.



Will Alex complete his evil plan? And the most important thing, will these boys get laid someday?



Javier Botet and David Pareja, two well known Spanish actors have been also involved in the filming.



Here you have links to the filming days

reviews.review:
Damn Virgins is one of those indie games that could only have emerged from a developer with a very specific vision and a willingness to embrace absurdity without hesitation. Developed and published by Luis Ruiz, this point-and-click adventure takes inspiration from the golden age of the genre while layering its own eccentric brand of humor on top. The result is a game that feels simultaneously nostalgic and bizarre, combining classic inventory puzzles, live-action sequences, and an intentionally over-the-top storyline involving ancient prophecies, university students, and a ritual sacrifice tied to the Mayan apocalypse. It is not a polished blockbuster by any means, but it never tries to be one. Instead, it thrives on personality and an undeniable enthusiasm for the adventure games that inspired it.

The plot centers on a university dean who becomes convinced that the world failed to end in 2012 because the Mayan gods were denied the sacrifices they demanded. His solution is to gather seven unsuspecting college virgins and prepare them for a ceremonial offering. From that premise alone, it is easy to tell whether Damn Virgins will appeal to a player or not. The writing constantly leans into its outrageous concept, delivering a mixture of pop culture references, awkward comedy, and playful self-awareness. While some jokes land better than others, the script maintains a consistent tone throughout its runtime. It rarely takes itself seriously, and that commitment to its comedic identity helps carry the experience even when individual scenes occasionally miss the mark.

Gameplay follows a traditional point-and-click structure that veterans of the genre will immediately recognize. Players explore environments, collect items, solve puzzles, and gradually uncover the mystery behind the dean's increasingly unhinged plans. The puzzle design is generally fair and avoids the infamous moon logic that plagued some older adventure titles, though experienced players may find the solutions somewhat predictable. The game values accessibility over complexity, making it approachable for newcomers while perhaps leaving genre enthusiasts wishing for more demanding challenges. Even so, progressing through the story remains enjoyable thanks to the steady pace of revelations and the game's willingness to surprise players with its unusual situations.

One of Damn Virgins' most memorable features is its use of live-action full-motion video sequences. These scenes punctuate major moments in the narrative and add a layer of charm that would have been impossible to achieve through the in-game engine alone. The performances are intentionally theatrical, often bordering on camp, which complements the game's overall presentation. Rather than feeling out of place, the FMV segments become part of the experience's identity. They reinforce the sense that this is a passion project unconcerned with conventional expectations. The inclusion of recognized Spanish actors also gives the production an extra touch of authenticity that elevates it above many small-scale indie releases.

Visually, the game shows its age and budget limitations. Character models are simple, animations can feel stiff, and some environments lack detail compared to modern standards. Navigation occasionally becomes cumbersome due to camera placement and movement restrictions, creating moments where interacting with objects feels less intuitive than it should. Fortunately, these shortcomings are somewhat offset by the game's strong sense of style. Its soundtrack keeps the atmosphere light and adventurous, and the colorful presentation suits the comedic tone. There is a sincerity to the overall package that makes it easier to overlook its technical imperfections.

What ultimately makes Damn Virgins worth remembering is its individuality. In an industry crowded with titles that often blend together, Luis Ruiz created something unmistakably his own. The game understands exactly what it wants to be: an affectionate tribute to classic adventure games wrapped in an outrageous comedy about destiny, friendship, and an exceptionally unfortunate group of college students. It will not appeal to everyone, particularly those looking for cutting-edge visuals or deeply intricate mechanics, but players who appreciate unconventional indie projects may find themselves pleasantly surprised by its charm.

Damn Virgins succeeds less because of technical excellence and more because of the enthusiasm embedded in every aspect of its design. It is the kind of game that reminds players why independent development remains important, offering ideas and experiences that larger studios would rarely attempt. More than a decade after its release, it remains an odd but memorable entry in the point-and-click genre, proving that sometimes originality can leave a stronger impression than perfection.

Rating: 7/10
